name: पुरुषोत्तमयोग
teaching: The world is an aśvattha tree grown upside down — roots above in the unseen, branches below nourished by the guṇas, and no end of it visible from inside. Krishna's instruction is severe and brief: cut it with the axe of non-attachment, then seek the place from which no one returns. A fragment of the divine lives as every soul; the whole exceeds both the perishable and the imperishable. An inverted tree, an axe of non-attachment, a fragment of God wearing senses, a fire digesting every meal — and above the perishable and imperishable alike, the Person this whole song belongs to.
questions: What are the deepest roots of your world-tree — the assumptions everything else branches from?
Non-attachment is called an axe, not a mood. What would one deliberate cut look like?
If a fragment of the supreme is living as you, how does that change what self-respect means?

verses.speaker: श्रीभगवानुवाच
verses.devanagari:
ऊर्ध्वमूलमधःशाखमश्वत्थं प्राहुरव्ययम् ।
छन्दांसि यस्य पर्णानि यस्तं वेद स वेदवित्॥
verses.transliteration:
ūrdhvamūlamadhaḥśākhamaśvatthaṃ prāhuravyayam
chandāṃsi yasya parṇāni yastaṃ veda sa vedavit
verses.essence: The Blessed Lord says: they speak of the imperishable ashvattha tree, its roots above, its branches below, whose leaves are the Vedic hymns. One who knows it is a knower of the Veda.
verses.translation: They (the wise) speak of the indestructible peepul tree having its root above and branches below, whose leaves are the metres or hymns: he who knows it is a knower of the Vedas.

anvaya.parts: ऊर्ध्व (above) + मूल (root): that whose root is above
अधस् (below) + शाखा (branch): that whose branches are below

anvaya.form: verb, perfect form with present sense, 3rd person plural
relative pronoun, masculine, genitive singular (of which)
verb, perfect form with present sense, 3rd person singular

anvaya.parts: वेद (Veda) + विद् (knower): one who knows the Veda

verses.explanation: The chapter opens with the strangest tree in scripture: an ashvattha, the sacred fig, growing upside down — rooted in the Above, branching downward into the world. Urdhva-mulam adhah-shakham is the image the Katha Upanishad (6.1) holds and the Gita unfolds. Nourishment flows from a root we cannot see, and what looks like the ground of things is actually the foliage. Chandamsi yasya parnani: the leaves are the Vedas themselves — even revelation belongs to the canopy, feeding the tree rather than being its root. Yas tam veda sa veda-vit: to know the tree's true orientation is to know what the Vedas are for.
verses.connection: Opens the chapter's master-image (15.1–4): existence as a tree to be understood, then felled.
verses.reflection: Picture the inverted tree once today: nourishment descending from a root above — and locate your sap.
verses.background: Krishna opens with the tradition's strangest tree: the eternal ashvattha with roots above and branches below, whose leaves are the Vedic hymns — its form not perceivable here, no end, no beginning, no resting place. Cut this firm-rooted tree with the strong axe of non-attachment, he commands, and seek that goal from which none return, surrendering to the primal Person.
verses.hook: What does the upside-down tree with roots above stand for?

refs.note: Describes the same eternal aśvattha tree with roots above and branches below.
Those who know the tree with upward roots do not believe death can end them.

views.text: The 'upward' root is Brahman with its unmanifest power of Māyā. Aśvattha is glossed as 'not lasting till tomorrow': a world perishing every moment, yet called imperishable because its flow has no beginning.
The root above is Brahmā the creator, seated above the worlds. The Vedas are the leaves because rites done for worldly desires make the tree flourish, yet the Vedas also teach how to fell it.

The root above is Puruṣottama, higher than perishable and imperishable. The chapter teaches knowledge seasoned with dispassion, because neither single-minded devotion nor knowledge is possible for one who is not detached.
The tree is only a metaphor; it is called eternal because nothing but the axe of knowledge can cut it, and it is the Lord's grace that removes the veil of ignorance.
The ever-changing world is a tree rooted in God, its leaves the Vedic rituals that keep souls cycling between heaven and earth; the true knower of the Vedas understands how to cut it down.

verses.devanagari:
अधश्चोर्ध्वं प्रसृतास्तस्य शाखा
गुणप्रवृद्धा विषयप्रवालाः ।
अधश्च मूलान्यनुसन्ततानि
कर्मानुबन्धीनि मनुष्यलोके॥
verses.transliteration:
adhaścordhvaṃ prasṛtāstasya śākhā guṇapravṛddhā viṣayapravālāḥ
adhaśca mūlānyanusantatāni karmānubandhīni manuṣyaloke
verses.essence: Below and above its branches spread, nourished by the gunas, with sense-objects for shoots; and downward its roots trail into the world of men, binding by action.
verses.translation: Below and above spread its branches, nourished by the Gunas; sense-objects are its buds; and below, in the world of men, stretch forth the roots, originating action.

anvaya.base: √सृ with प्र · to flow forth, extend
anvaya.form: past participle, feminine, nominative plural (agrees with branches)

anvaya.parts: गुण (quality of nature) + प्रवृद्ध (grown strong): grown strong by the gunas
विषय (sense-object) + प्रवाल (young shoot): whose shoots are sense-objects

anvaya.base: √तन् with अनु + सम् · to stretch, extend

anvaya.parts: कर्म (action) + अनुबन्धिन् (binding, followed by): which bind one to action, with action following
मनुष्य (human) + लोक (world): the world of humans

verses.explanation: The botany of bondage: branches fattened by the three gunas of chapter 14, tipped with viṣaya-pravālāḥ — sense-objects as tender new shoots, each enticement a fresh bud. And a second root-system: aerial roots, like the banyan's, dropping back down into human life and re-anchoring there as karma. The tree propagates through our actions; every grasping deed is a root striking soil.
verses.connection: Maps ch14's gunas onto the tree: how the world-growth feeds, buds, and re-roots itself in us.
verses.reflection: Spot one fresh bud of enticement today — a viṣaya-shoot — and watch it without watering it.
verses.background: Krishna opens with the tradition's strangest tree: the eternal ashvattha with roots above and branches below, whose leaves are the Vedic hymns — its form not perceivable here, no end, no beginning, no resting place. Cut this firm-rooted tree with the strong axe of non-attachment, he commands, and seek that goal from which none return, surrendering to the primal Person.
verses.hook: What feeds the branches and roots of the world-tree?

views.text: The secondary roots are latent impressions of attraction and repulsion born of past action. They spread above all in the human world, because only humans are qualified for rites and duties.
As a tree's leaves show its girth, fruit and taste, the Vedic hymns point to Brahman; the roots spreading below are good and bad actions.

Wrongdoers spread downward into animal births and the virtuous upward into divine ones. The one main root is the Lord; these lesser roots are desires for particular enjoyments, which bind through action.
The three qualities water the tree; sense objects are its buds, sprouting desires like a banyan's aerial roots, and acting on them makes the tree spread and entangles the soul further.

verses.devanagari:
न रूपमस्येह तथोपलभ्यते
नान्तो न चादिर्न च सम्प्रतिष्ठा ।
अश्वत्थमेनं सुविरूढमूल-
मसङ्गशस्त्रेण दृढेन छित्त्वा॥
verses.transliteration:
na rūpamasyeha tathopalabhyate nānto na cādirna ca sampratiṣṭhā
aśvatthamenaṃ suvirūḍhamūlamasaṅgaśastreṇa dṛḍhena chittvā
verses.essence: Its form is not perceived here as such — not its end, nor its beginning, nor its foundation. Having cut this firm-rooted ashvattha with the strong axe of non-attachment —
verses.translation: Its form is not perceived here as such, neither its end nor its origin, nor its foundation nor resting place: having cut asunder this firmly rooted peepul tree with the strong axe of non-attachment.

anvaya.parts: सु (well) + विरूढ (grown) + मूल (root): whose roots have grown deep

anvaya.form: compound noun, neuter, instrumental singular (by means of)
anvaya.parts: असङ्ग (non-attachment) + शस्त्र (weapon, blade): the weapon that is non-attachment

anvaya.form: adjective, neuter, instrumental singular (by means of)

verses.explanation: Standing inside the canopy, no one can see the whole tree — no edge, no origin, no trunk to point to; we are leaves trying to survey the forest. So the instruction is not to map it but to fell it: asaṅga-śastreṇa, with the axe of non-attachment, dṛḍhena, swung firm. The one tree in scripture that is sacred *and* must be cut down — because what it grows is entanglement.
verses.connection: The image turns from contemplation to action: the unsurveyable tree meets the axe of 15.3–4.
verses.reflection: Stop trying to map the whole forest today; sharpen the axe of non-attachment on one branch instead.
verses.background: Krishna opens with the tradition's strangest tree: the eternal ashvattha with roots above and branches below, whose leaves are the Vedic hymns — its form not perceivable here, no end, no beginning, no resting place. Cut this firm-rooted tree with the strong axe of non-attachment, he commands, and seek that goal from which none return, surrendering to the primal Person.
verses.hook: With what can the tree of worldly existence be cut down?

refs.note: The soul, forgetful of God, is lifted to heaven and dropped to hell by material energy, showing the endless tossing within this tree.

views.text: Its form is not grasped because, like a dream or a mirage, it is gone as soon as it is seen. The sword of detachment is hardened by resolve toward the Self and sharpened by repeated discrimination.
People in saṃsāra perceive only 'I am a man, son of so-and-so'. They miss that attachment to the guṇas is the tree's beginning and that ignorance, taking the body for the self, is its support.
Asaṅga means giving up 'I' and 'mine'; the strong weapon is right inquiry, which cuts the tree away from oneself.
Souls lured by sense objects and rituals are tossed up and down through births; the tree can be felled only with the axe of detachment, which grows from knowing oneself as an eternal soul.

verses.devanagari:
ततः पदं तत्परिमार्गितव्यं
यस्मिन्गता न निवर्तन्ति भूयः ।
तमेव चाद्यं पुरुषं प्रपद्ये ।
यतः प्रवृत्तिः प्रसृता पुराणी॥
verses.transliteration:
tataḥ padaṃ tatparimārgitavyaṃ yasmingatā na nivartanti bhūyaḥ
tameva cādyaṃ puruṣaṃ prapadye
yataḥ pravṛttiḥ prasṛtā purāṇī
verses.essence: — then that goal must be sought, going to which none return again: 'I take refuge in that primal Purusha from whom the ancient current streamed forth.'
verses.translation: Then That goal should be sought for, whither having gone none returns again. I seek refuge in that Primeval Purusha Whence streamed forth the ancient activity or energy.

anvaya.form: gerundive (must be done), neuter, nominative singular

anvaya.base: √पद् with प्र · to go to, take refuge
anvaya.form: verb, present, middle voice, 1st person singular

verses.explanation: After the felling, the seeking — and the verse hands the seeker the exact words: tam eva cādyaṁ puruṣaṁ prapadye, *I take refuge in the primal Person*. A mantra of surrender embedded mid-teaching, present tense, first person, ready to say. The destination is defined by its one-way door: yasmin gatā na nivartanti, no return — the same promise as 8.21, now reached by axe and refuge together.
verses.connection: Completes the tree-teaching: cut the growth, then trace the sap back to the root and surrender there.
verses.reflection: Say the planted mantra once, slowly: I take refuge in that primal Purusha — and mean the present tense.
verses.background: Krishna opens with the tradition's strangest tree: the eternal ashvattha with roots above and branches below, whose leaves are the Vedic hymns — its form not perceivable here, no end, no beginning, no resting place. Cut this firm-rooted tree with the strong axe of non-attachment, he commands, and seek that goal from which none return, surrendering to the primal Person.
verses.hook: Once the tree is cut, what should one seek and take refuge in?

views.text: The state to be sought is Viṣṇu's. The seeking itself takes the form of refuge, 'I take refuge in that primeval Person', from whom the world-tree came forth like a magician's illusion.
Reads prapadye as an instruction: one should take refuge in the Primal Person alone, because the ancient flow of attachment to the guṇas streamed from Him and only He can end it.
The search for the root-state is carried out by single-minded devotion: one seeks it by saying, 'I go for refuge to that primal Person from whom this ancient flow spread.'
After cutting the tree with detachment, one must seek and surrender to God, its root, the source from whom all creation flows, reaching whom there is no return.

verses.devanagari:
निर्मानमोहा जितसङ्गदोषा
अध्यात्मनित्या विनिवृत्तकामाः ।
द्वन्द्वैर्विमुक्ताः सुखदुःखसंज्ञैर्-
गच्छन्त्यमूढाः पदमव्ययं तत्॥
verses.transliteration:
nirmānamohā jitasaṅgadoṣā adhyātmanityā vinivṛttakāmāḥ
dvandvairvimuktāḥ sukhaduḥkhasaṃjñairgacchantyamūḍhāḥ padamavyayaṃ tat
verses.essence: Free of pride and delusion, the fault of attachment conquered, ever dwelling in the Self, desires fully turned away, released from the pairs called pleasure and pain — the undeluded reach that imperishable goal.
verses.translation: Free from pride and delusion, victorious over the evil of attachment, dwelling constantly in the Self, their desires having completely turned away, freed from the pairs of opposites known as pleasure and pain, the undeluded reach the eternal goal.

anvaya.parts: निर् (without) + मान (pride) + मोह (delusion): those from whom pride and delusion have gone
जित (conquered) + सङ्ग (attachment) + दोष (fault): those by whom the fault of attachment is conquered
अध्यात्म (the inner Self) + नित्य (constant): those constantly given to the Self
विनिवृत्त (fully turned away) + काम (desire): those whose desires have turned away

anvaya.form: compound adjective, neuter, instrumental plural (agrees with the pairs)
anvaya.parts: सुख (pleasure) + दुःख (pain) + संज्ञा (name): which are called pleasure and pain

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, masculine, nominative plural (subject)
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + मूढ (deluded): those not deluded

verses.explanation: The traveler's profile for the road of 15.4, in a single breath. Most of the list is something put down: pride and delusion, the fault of clinging, craving, the seesaw of the pairs called pleasure and pain. One item is held instead: adhyātma-nityāḥ, ever dwelling in the Self. The journey to the imperishable is packed mostly by unpacking, and what remains is steady attention to the Self. Amūḍhāḥ, the undeluded, names the result: clear sight.
verses.connection: Lists the equipment for 15.4's seeking — almost all of it subtraction, plus constancy in the Self.
verses.reflection: Pack for the journey by unpacking today: set down pride, delusion, clinging — travel light.
verses.background: The travelers and the destination are described in two breaths: free of pride and delusion, attachment conquered, desires stilled, released from the pairs of pleasure and pain, the undeluded reach the imperishable goal — which neither sun nor moon nor fire illumines; having gone there, none return; that is My supreme abode.
verses.hook: Who reaches the eternal state from which there is no return?

refs.note: The material world is one part of creation, while three parts are God's eternal abode beyond birth and death.
All moving and unmoving beings are servants of Lord Nārāyaṇa, the controller of the world.

views.text: In jita-saṅga-doṣa, association itself is the fault. Vinivṛtta-kāmāḥ are those whose desires have gone without trace: the self-controlled, the monks.
Free of pride and delusion means no longer mistaking the body for the self. For those who take refuge in the Lord, every step until perfection becomes easy by His grace.
Saṅga is the notion 'I am the doer', and likes and dislikes are its faults; one who stays even before pleasant and unpleasant objects has conquered it.
Surrender begins by dropping the pride of being the enjoyer and growing a desire to serve God; souls purified this way enter his eternal realm and remain there forever.

verses.devanagari:
न तद्भासयते सूर्यो न शशाङ्को न पावकः ।
यद्गत्वा न निवर्तन्ते तद्धाम परमं मम॥
verses.transliteration:
na tadbhāsayate sūryo na śaśāṅko na pāvakaḥ
yadgatvā na nivartante taddhāma paramaṃ mama
verses.essence: Neither sun nor moon nor fire illumines it. Having gone there, none return: that is my supreme abode.
verses.translation: Neither doth the sun illumine there nor the moon, nor the fire; having gone thither they return not; that is My supreme abode.

anvaya.form: verb, causative (makes shine), present, 3rd person singular

anvaya.parts: शश (hare) + अङ्क (mark): the one marked with a hare

anvaya.form: relative pronoun, neuter, accusative singular (object of going)
verb, present, middle voice, 3rd person plural

verses.explanation: The destination described by what it does not need: sun, moon, fire — the three lamps of the manifest world — all unemployed there, because it is the light they borrow from. Here the Gita echoes the Upanishads' great verse (Katha, Mundaka), na tatra sūryo bhāti. Where light itself is at home, nothing needs lighting; and from home, no one commutes back.
verses.connection: Names the journey's end — mama dhāma, *my* abode — and quietly personalizes the Upanishadic absolute.
verses.reflection: Spend a minute on the light that lamps cannot reach — sun, moon, fire all unemployed there.
verses.background: The travelers and the destination are described in two breaths: free of pride and delusion, attachment conquered, desires stilled, released from the pairs of pleasure and pain, the undeluded reach the imperishable goal — which neither sun nor moon nor fire illumines; having gone there, none return; that is My supreme abode.
verses.hook: What is Krishna's abode like, which no sun or moon lights?

refs.note: Golok, Krishna's own abode, lies in the spiritual sky along with the abodes of other divine forms.
Govinda dwells in Golok with Rādhā and his eternal associates, enlivened by blissful spiritual energy.

views.text: 'That' points to the Abode, which is itself light: the state of Viṣṇu that sun, moon and fire cannot illumine, though they illumine everything else.
The supreme light here is the self's own knowledge, which reveals even the sun; outer lights only remove the darkness between senses and objects. This self is the Lord's glory, and so 'Mine'.
Sun, moon and fire are bound by time, are objects of knowledge and serve the senses. That is the knower itself, beyond space and time, which moves the senses and transcends them.
God's abode is self-luminous, made of his spiritual energy and free of defects; souls who reach it live there eternally and share in his divine pastimes.

verses.devanagari:
ममैवांशो जीवलोके जीवभूतः सनातनः ।
मनःषष्ठानीन्द्रियाणि प्रकृतिस्थानि कर्षति॥
verses.transliteration:
mamaivāṃśo jīvaloke jīvabhūtaḥ sanātanaḥ
manaḥṣaṣṭhānīndriyāṇi prakṛtisthāni karṣati
verses.essence: A fragment of my very self, become the eternal living soul in the world of life, draws to itself the senses, with mind as the sixth, which rest in prakriti.
verses.translation: An eternal portion of Myself having become a living soul in the world of life, draws to (itself) the (five) senses with the mind for the sixth, abiding in Nature.

anvaya.meaning: in the world of living beings
anvaya.parts: जीव (living being) + लोक (world): the world of living beings
जीव (living soul) + भूत (become): that which has become the soul
मनस् (mind) + षष्ठ (sixth): those of which the mind is the sixth
प्रकृति (nature, matter) + स्थ (standing in): which rest in prakriti

verses.explanation: The verse that names what you are: mamaivāṁśaḥ — a fragment, a portion, of *me*, become the living soul in the world of life. Sanātanaḥ, eternal, is the word the debates turn on: Ramanuja takes the portion as real and everlasting; Shankara takes the partition as appearance, like space enclosed in a jar. Then the embodiment mechanism in one verb: karṣati, the soul *draws* — pulls mind and the five senses around itself like a magnet gathering filings, and a person assembles. Whichever metaphysics, the daily fact stands: the divine portion in you is what gathers a mind and senses and calls the bundle a person.
verses.connection: The chapter's anthropology: after the cosmic tree, the soul itself — divine in substance, derivative in scale.
verses.reflection: Carry your pedigree through one hard hour: an eternal fragment of His very self — that is the traveler.
verses.background: Krishna turns to the traveler itself: an eternal fragment of My very self, become the living soul, draws to itself mind and the five senses; taking a body and leaving it, the lord of the body carries these along as wind carries fragrance from their seats. The deluded do not perceive him departing or dwelling; those with the eye of knowledge see — the striving yogis behold him in themselves; the unrefined, though striving, see him not.
verses.hook: What are living beings, in their relation to Krishna?

refs.note: The senses were made to turn outward toward the world, which is why bound souls struggle with them.

views.text: The 'part' is like the sun reflected in water or space enclosed in a pot: imagined as a part through an adjunct of ignorance, it merges back when the adjunct is removed, which is why there is no return.
Though an everlasting part of the Lord, the self becomes bound by beginningless karma, contracted in power and knowledge, and gathers the mind and senses that belong to bodies made of Prakṛti.
Answers a doubt: if all merge in the Lord in deep sleep and dissolution, who transmigrates? The portion veiled by ignorance draws the senses, latent in prakṛti, back out for enjoyment.
Souls are separated parts of God, distinct from his direct forms; those bound in the world since eternity struggle with the mind and five senses.

verses.devanagari:
शरीरं यदवाप्नोति यच्चाप्युत्क्रामतीश्वरः ।
गृहीत्वैतानि संयाति वायुर्गन्धानिवाशयात्॥
verses.transliteration:
śarīraṃ yadavāpnoti yaccāpyutkrāmatīśvaraḥ
gṛhītvaitāni saṃyāti vāyurgandhānivāśayāt
verses.essence: When the lord of the body takes on a body, and when he leaves it, he departs taking these along — as the wind carries scents from their dwelling-places.
verses.translation: When the Lord (as the individual soul) obtains a body and when He leaves it, He takes these and goes (with them) as the wind takes the scents from their seats (flowers, etc.).

anvaya.form: relative pronoun, neuter, used as indeclinable (when)
relative pronoun, neuter, used as indeclinable (when)

anvaya.base: √क्रम् with उत् · to step out, leave

verses.explanation: Transmigration in a single fragrance: vāyur gandhān ivāśayāt — as wind lifts perfume from a flower bed and carries it elsewhere, the soul lifts mind and senses from the dying body and moves on. The scent is invisible, weightless, yet unmistakably *that garden's*. What travels between lives is just so: no luggage, only the subtle signature of all one has been.
verses.connection: Shows 15.7's gathered instruments in transit — the mechanics of rebirth, rendered as perfume.
verses.reflection: Notice what subtle scent you would carry from this chapter of life — the wind takes only fragrance.
verses.background: Krishna turns to the traveler itself: an eternal fragment of My very self, become the living soul, draws to itself mind and the five senses; taking a body and leaving it, the lord of the body carries these along as wind carries fragrance from their seats. The deluded do not perceive him departing or dwelling; those with the eye of knowledge see — the striving yogis behold him in themselves; the unrefined, though striving, see him not.
verses.hook: What does the soul carry with it when it leaves a body?

views.text: Takes the second quarter first: when the soul leaves a body it draws out the organs, then carries them wholly into the next body, as wind carries scents away from flowers.
The self takes the senses along with the subtle elements, as the wind lifts subtle particles of scent from garlands, sandal and musk and moves elsewhere.
As the breeze carries fragrance, the soul at death carries its subtle body, mind and senses with their impressions into the next body, which may explain why people born blind still dream.

verses.devanagari:
श्रोत्रं चक्षुः स्पर्शनं च रसनं घ्राणमेव च ।
अधिष्ठाय मनश्चायं विषयानुपसेवते॥
verses.transliteration:
śrotraṃ cakṣuḥ sparśanaṃ ca rasanaṃ ghrāṇameva ca
adhiṣṭhāya manaścāyaṃ viṣayānupasevate
verses.essence: Presiding over hearing, sight, touch, taste and smell, and over the mind, this one savors the objects of the senses.
verses.translation: Presiding over the ear, the eye, touch, taste and smell, as well as the mind, it enjoys the objects of the senses.

anvaya.base: √स्था with अधि · to stand over, govern

anvaya.form: verb, present, middle voice, 3rd person singular

verses.explanation: The fragment settles into its new instrument and the concert begins: adhiṣṭhāya, presiding — the soul as the one audience for whom five senses and a mind perform the world. Every flavor, every birdsong, every touch is staged for this hidden enjoyer. The verse holds no rebuke; it simply identifies who is actually tasting your tea.
verses.connection: The soul installed and operating — which makes 15.10's blindness to it all the stranger.
verses.reflection: Identify the real taster of your tea once today: the hidden enjoyer presiding over the senses.
verses.background: Krishna turns to the traveler itself: an eternal fragment of My very self, become the living soul, draws to itself mind and the five senses; taking a body and leaving it, the lord of the body carries these along as wind carries fragrance from their seats. The deluded do not perceive him departing or dwelling; those with the eye of knowledge see — the striving yogis behold him in themselves; the unrefined, though striving, see him not.
verses.hook: Through what does the self enjoy the world of the senses?

refs.note: Tulsidas prays that Rām be as constantly dear to him as a woman is to the lustful and money to the greedy.

views.text: Seated in the body, the embodied one enjoys sound and the other objects by presiding over ear, eye, skin, tongue and nose, and the mind as the sixth, each together with its organ.
Presiding over the senses, the lord of the body drives each organ toward its own object, sound and the rest, and so enjoys them.
The soul uses the mind together with each sense in turn to experience sound, touch, form, taste and smell; this is the subtle body at work within the gross body.
The soul tastes the world through mind and senses, but being divine it is never satisfied by material pleasure; turning those same senses toward God, as Tulsidas did, ends the search.

verses.devanagari:
उत्क्रामन्तं स्थितं वापि भुञ्जानं वा गुणान्वितम् ।
विमूढा नानुपश्यन्ति पश्यन्ति ज्ञानचक्षुषः॥
verses.transliteration:
utkrāmantaṃ sthitaṃ vāpi bhuñjānaṃ vā guṇānvitam
vimūḍhā nānupaśyanti paśyanti jñānacakṣuṣaḥ
verses.essence: Whether departing, staying, or experiencing, joined with the gunas — the deluded do not perceive him. Those with the eye of knowledge see.
verses.translation: The deluded do not see Him Who departs, stays and enjoys; but they who possess the eye of knowledge behold Him.

anvaya.base: √क्रम् with उत् · to step out, leave

anvaya.parts: गुण (quality of nature) + अन्वित (accompanied by): accompanied by the gunas

anvaya.form: past participle used as noun, masculine, nominative plural (subject)

anvaya.meaning: those with the eye of knowledge
anvaya.parts: ज्ञान (knowledge) + चक्षुस् (eye): those whose eye is knowledge

verses.explanation: The strangest blindness: the soul is the nearest fact there is — it is doing the looking — and precisely so, the deluded never notice it, in life, in experience, even at the bedside of death. Like the eye that sees everything but itself. The remedy is named from 13.35: jñāna-cakṣus, the knowledge-eye, which turns perception around to catch the perceiver.
verses.connection: The visibility problem: the divine fragment of 15.7 hides in plain sight as the seer itself.
verses.reflection: Turn perception around once today and try to catch the perceiver — the nearest hide in plain sight.
verses.background: Krishna turns to the traveler itself: an eternal fragment of My very self, become the living soul, draws to itself mind and the five senses; taking a body and leaving it, the lord of the body carries these along as wind carries fragrance from their seats. The deluded do not perceive him departing or dwelling; those with the eye of knowledge see — the striving yogis behold him in themselves; the unrefined, though striving, see him not.
verses.hook: Why do most people fail to see the self in the body?

views.text: Though the self is most within reach, those whose hearts are dragged by enjoyments do not see it, and the Lord laments this. The eye of knowledge is scripture supported by reasoning.
The deluded take the body for the self. Those with the eye of knowledge see the self as distinct from the body in every state: departing, staying, enjoying.
The senses turn outward, so people see the world and not the Self within; as Yama told Naciketas, the wise turn their gaze inward.
The soul is spiritual and cannot be detected by material instruments, so the deluded take the body for the self; only the eye of knowledge sees that the soul gives the body life.

verses.devanagari:
यतन्तो योगिनश्चैनं पश्यन्त्यात्मन्यवस्थितम् ।
यतन्तोऽप्यकृतात्मानो नैनं पश्यन्त्यचेतसः॥
verses.transliteration:
yatanto yoginaścainaṃ paśyantyātmanyavasthitam
yatanto'pyakṛtātmāno nainaṃ paśyantyacetasaḥ
verses.essence: Striving yogis behold him established in the self; but the unrefined, the unmindful, though striving, see him not.
verses.translation: The Yogins striving (for perfection) behold Him dwelling in the Self; but, the unrefined and unintelligent, even though striving, see Him not.

anvaya.base: √स्था with अव · to stay, be settled

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + कृत (made, refined) + आत्मन् (self): those whose self is not made ready
अ (without) + चेतस् (mind, discernment): those lacking discernment

verses.explanation: A precision about effort: yatanto 'pi — *even striving*, some see nothing. The variable is akṛtātmānaḥ, the un-made self: effort poured into an unprepared instrument is rain on stone. The twenty marks of 13.8–12 were the making; vision is what a made self does naturally. Practice without purification gathers technique and misses the point.
verses.connection: Qualifies 15.10's knowledge-eye: it must be grown in a refined self, not merely exercised.
verses.reflection: Pair your striving with refining today — effort lands only in a made self; polish the instrument.
verses.background: Krishna turns to the traveler itself: an eternal fragment of My very self, become the living soul, draws to itself mind and the five senses; taking a body and leaving it, the lord of the body carries these along as wind carries fragrance from their seats. The deluded do not perceive him departing or dwelling; those with the eye of knowledge see — the striving yogis behold him in themselves; the unrefined, though striving, see him not.
verses.hook: Why do some who strive see the self while others never do?

views.text: The diligent yogis see the Self in their own intellect and realize 'I am This'. The unpurified, proud and restless do not see it, even when they strive with scripture and other means of knowledge.
The striving are karma-yogis who have practised self-surrender to the Lord and so purified their minds; those who do not take refuge in Him cannot see the self as distinct from the body.
Effort by one whose passion has not decayed bears no fruit, like seed sown out of season: water and soil alone do not make a harvest.
Effort must go in the right direction: judging the divine by material senses and intellect is the well-frog's mistake, while a heart purified by humility and faith naturally perceives the soul.

verses.devanagari:
यदादित्यगतं तेजो जगद्भासयतेऽखिलम् ।
यच्चन्द्रमसि यच्चाग्नौ तत्तेजो विद्धि मामकम्॥
verses.transliteration:
yadādityagataṃ tejo jagadbhāsayate'khilam
yaccandramasi yaccāgnau tattejo viddhi māmakam
verses.essence: The splendor residing in the sun, which illumines the entire world, and that in the moon and in fire — know that splendor as mine.
verses.translation: That light which residing in the sun illumines the whole world, that which is in the moon and in the fire know that light to be Mine.

anvaya.parts: आदित्य (sun) + गत (gone into, present in): that which is in the sun

anvaya.form: verb, causative (makes shine), present, 3rd person singular

verses.explanation: The chapter turns outward: the three great lights that 15.6 said cannot reach his abode are now claimed as his projections — every lumen in the visible universe drawn from one account. The teaching method is immersive: for the next four verses, wherever Arjuna's senses land — light, earth, food, memory — they will be told whose presence they are touching.
verses.connection: Begins the immanence-litany (15.12–15): the Purushottama located in daylight, soil, digestion, and thought.
verses.reflection: Read every lumen today off one account: sun, moon, fire — splendor on loan from a single source.
verses.background: The immanence litany of the chapter: the splendor in sun, moon, and fire is Mine; entering the earth I support beings; becoming the moon I nourish the plants; as the fire of life in every body I digest the fourfold food; and seated in every heart I give memory, knowledge, and their taking away — by all the Vedas I alone am to be known, the maker and knower of Vedanta.
verses.hook: Whose light shines in the sun, the moon and fire?

refs.note: Its story of the gods humbled before a mysterious being shows that all their power, like the sun's light, comes from God.

views.text: Tejas can be the light of consciousness. It is named in sun, moon and fire because sattva abounds there, just as a face appears clearly only in a clean mirror.
The power of illumining is granted to the sun and the other lights by the Lord, whom each of them has worshipped.
Verses 12–14 teach that the power of the elements, together and singly, to sustain the world is the Lord's own power; sunlight both illumines and sustains.
The radiance of sun, moon and fire is God's energy; forgetting this, we grow proud of borrowed powers, as the gods did in the Kena story.

verses.devanagari:
गामाविश्य च भूतानि धारयाम्यहमोजसा ।
पुष्णामि चौषधीः सर्वाः सोमो भूत्वा रसात्मकः॥
verses.transliteration:
gāmāviśya ca bhūtāni dhārayāmyahamojasā
puṣṇāmi cauṣadhīḥ sarvāḥ somo bhūtvā rasātmakaḥ
verses.essence: Entering the earth, I sustain all beings by my power; and becoming the sap-rich soma, I nourish all the herbs.
verses.translation: Permeating the earth I support all beings by (My) energy; and having become the watery moon I nourish all herbs.

anvaya.form: verb, causative form, present, 1st person singular
noun, neuter, instrumental singular (by means of)

anvaya.parts: रस (sap, juice) + आत्मक (having the nature of): whose nature is sap

verses.explanation: From light to ground: the planet's very holding-together is his ojas, and the moon — soma, lord of sap in Vedic physiology — is his nourishing mode, swelling the herbs with juice by night. Agriculture becomes theology: the wheat ripens because someone is in the field, in the moonlight, in the rising water of the stalk.
verses.connection: The litany descends from sky to soil — and prepares the most intimate claim of all in 15.14.
verses.reflection: Walk on the earth once today aware of what holds it together — and what swells the green things by night.
verses.background: The immanence litany of the chapter: the splendor in sun, moon, and fire is Mine; entering the earth I support beings; becoming the moon I nourish the plants; as the fire of life in every body I digest the fourfold food; and seated in every heart I give memory, knowledge, and their taking away — by all the Vedas I alone am to be known, the maker and knower of Vedanta.
verses.hook: What sustains the earth's creatures and nourishes its plants?

views.text: Ojas is God's power, free of passion, that enters the earth so the heavy earth neither falls nor crumbles. Soma, source of all juices, fills plants like rice and barley with flavour.
Moonlight both illumines and nourishes because earth, water and fire are joined in it with the Lord; hence the moon is named for light in 15.12 and for nourishing sap here.
God's energy makes the earth fit for life, through countless finely tuned conditions, and gives moonlight the nourishing power that sustains all plant life.

verses.devanagari:
अहं वैश्वानरो भूत्वा प्राणिनां देहमाश्रितः ।
प्राणापानसमायुक्तः पचाम्यन्नं चतुर्विधम्॥
verses.transliteration:
ahaṃ vaiśvānaro bhūtvā prāṇināṃ dehamāśritaḥ
prāṇāpānasamāyuktaḥ pacāmyannaṃ caturvidham
verses.essence: Becoming the fire of life in the bodies of breathing beings, joined with the in-breath and out-breath, I digest the four kinds of food.
verses.translation: Having become the fire Vaisvanara, I abide in the body of living beings and, associated with the Prana and the Apana, digest the fourfold food.

anvaya.base: वैश्वानर · universal fire; fire in the body
√श्रि with आ · to resort to, dwell in
प्राणापानसमायुक्त · joined with prana and apana
anvaya.parts: प्राण (upward breath) + अपान (downward breath) + समायुक्त (joined): united with prana and apana
चतुर् (four) + विधा (kind): of four kinds

verses.explanation: The litany arrives inside the belly: vaiśvānara, the universal fire, here the gastric flame itself, working the bellows of prāṇa and apāna to cook the four foods — chewed, drunk, licked, sucked. The God of the thousand suns of chapter 11, found again as the warmth in your stomach after lunch. Many recite this verse before meals: digestion acknowledged as the nearest daily miracle.
verses.connection: Immanence at its most domestic: the cosmic fire as the body's own hearth.
verses.reflection: Before one meal today, greet the vaishvanara fire — the cosmic flame doing your digestion.
verses.background: The immanence litany of the chapter: the splendor in sun, moon, and fire is Mine; entering the earth I support beings; becoming the moon I nourish the plants; as the fire of life in every body I digest the fourfold food; and seated in every heart I give memory, knowledge, and their taking away — by all the Vedas I alone am to be known, the maker and knower of Vedanta.
verses.hook: What power inside the body digests the food you eat?

refs.note: Says God is the fire within a person by which food is digested.

views.text: The eater is the fire Vaiśvānara and the eaten is Soma, the food; one who sees all that exists as these two is not touched by impurity in food.
Soma and the digestive fire are the Lord's glories; 'becoming Soma' and 'becoming the fire' identify them with Him by co-ordinate predication, as His own.
Spells out the four foods: chewed with the teeth like cakes, swallowed with the tongue like porridge, licked slowly like molasses, and pressed for juice like sugarcane.
God dwells in all beings as the digestive fire; through this, the earth and plant life, he supports every part of our existence.

verses.devanagari:
सर्वस्य चाहं हृदि सन्निविष्टो
मत्तः स्मृतिर्ज्ञानमपोहनञ्च ।
वेदैश्च सर्वैरहमेव वेद्यो
वेदान्तकृद्वेदविदेव चाहम्॥
verses.transliteration:
sarvasya cāhaṃ hṛdi sanniviṣṭo mattaḥ smṛtirjñānamapohanañca
vedaiśca sarvairahameva vedyo vedāntakṛdvedavideva cāham
verses.essence: And I am seated in the hearts of all; from me come memory, knowledge, and their loss. By all the Vedas it is I who am to be known; I am the maker of Vedanta, and the knower of the Veda am I.
verses.translation: And I am seated in the hearts of all; from Me are memory and knowledge, as well as their absence. I am verily That which has to be known by all the Vedas; I am indeed the author of the Vedanta and the knower of the Vedas am I.

anvaya.base: √विश् with सम् + नि · to enter, settle

anvaya.form: pronoun with -tas ending, ablative sense (from me)
gerundive (to be done), masculine, nominative singular

anvaya.parts: वेद (Veda) + अन्त (end) + कृत् (maker): the one who made the Veda's conclusion
वेद (Veda) + विद् (knower): one who knows the Veda

verses.explanation: The litany's summit, and one of the Gita's most quoted verses. Sarvasya chaham hridi sannivishtah: seated in every heart, he is the source of smṛti and jñāna, memory and knowledge — and, startlingly, of apohanam, their loss. The commentaries pause at the third: even the veiling is his office, which is why only he can lift it. Then the hermeneutic master key: vedaish cha sarvair aham eva vedyah — all scripture, read to its end, is about him. He made its conclusion (vedānta-kṛt) and knows what every verse was for (veda-vit): the one reading it from within.
verses.connection: Closes the litany at its center — the heart — and sets up the final doctrine of the two-plus-one purushas.
verses.reflection: Sit with the heart-resident a moment: source of your memory, your knowledge — and yes, your forgetting.
verses.background: The immanence litany of the chapter: the splendor in sun, moon, and fire is Mine; entering the earth I support beings; becoming the moon I nourish the plants; as the fire of life in every body I digest the fourfold food; and seated in every heart I give memory, knowledge, and their taking away — by all the Vedas I alone am to be known, the maker and knower of Vedanta.
verses.hook: Where do memory, knowledge and forgetting come from?

refs.note: All the Vedas point toward God, the goal named in this verse.
Knowledge in living beings arises from God, and by his power it is taken away.

views.text: Memory and knowledge come from the Self to those of good deeds, and their loss to those of evil deeds; vedānta-kṛt means the source of the Vedānta teaching tradition.
Apohana is the cessation of knowledge, or else ūha, the reasoning that tests whether a means of knowledge applies; vedānta-kṛt means He brings the Vedas' rites to fruition.

The heart of all is free awareness, the I-consciousness. From it come knowing, which creates anew; differentiating, which limits and makes the bound soul; and remembering, which re-illumines stored impressions.
The Lord is what all the Vedas teach, under the forms of their various deities, and as vedānta-kṛt He is the guru who starts the teaching lineage and gives knowledge.
God gives us memory, knowledge and even forgetting, and he is the author, knower and goal of the Vedas; all ritual and study is worthless unless it leads to loving him.

verses.devanagari:
द्वाविमौ पुरुषौ लोके क्षरश्चाक्षर एव च ।
क्षरः सर्वाणि भूतानि कूटस्थोऽक्षर उच्यते॥
verses.transliteration:
dvāvimau puruṣau loke kṣaraścākṣara eva ca
kṣaraḥ sarvāṇi bhūtāni kūṭastho'kṣara ucyate
verses.essence: There are these two purushas in the world: the perishable and the imperishable. The perishable is all beings; the unchanging one is called the imperishable.
verses.translation: Two Purushas there are in this world, the perishable and the imperishable. All beings are the perishable and the Kutastha the unchanging is called the imperishable.

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, masculine, nominative singular
adjective used as noun, masculine, nominative singular
anvaya.parts: अ (not) + क्षर (perishing): the not-perishing

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, masculine, nominative singular (subject)
compound adjective used as noun, masculine, nominative singular (subject)
anvaya.parts: कूट (anvil, peak, heap) + स्थ (standing): one who stands fixed like an anvil or a peak

anvaya.form: adjective used as noun, masculine, nominative singular

verses.explanation: The final taxonomy begins: kṣara, the perishable — every form, every body, the whole flowing world of beings; and akṣara, the kūṭastha — the anvil-still, unchanging one. Who that second 'person' is, the commentators dispute: Śaṅkara takes it as Māyā, the imperishable seed of the world-tree; Rāmānuja as the liberated selves; Śrīdhara as the conscious enjoyer who stays unchanged while bodies perish. Either way the count seems complete: the changing and the unchanging, two. The next verse adds what neither category expected.
verses.connection: Names the perishable and the imperishable — the setup for 15.17's third term.
verses.reflection: Sort one hour of your world into kshara and akshara — the flowing and the unmoved watching it flow.
verses.background: The summit of the chapter and one of the Gita's peaks: two Persons in the world, the perishable (all beings) and the imperishable (the unchanging) — but there is another, the Highest, called Paramatma, the imperishable Lord who enters and sustains the three worlds. Because I transcend the perishable and exceed even the imperishable, I am celebrated as Purushottama. Who knows Me thus, undeluded, worships Me with his whole being — and with this most secret teaching declared, one becomes wise and fulfilled.
verses.hook: What are the two kinds of beings Krishna names in this world?

views.text: The kūṭastha is Māyā, the Lord's power and the seed of all that perishes. Both are 'persons' only figuratively, as limiting adjuncts of the supreme Person.
Kṣara is all selves bound with matter, from Brahmā to a blade of grass; akṣara is the liberated self, free of matter, named in the singular as a class, not as one soul.
The undiscerning call only bodies 'person'; the kūṭastha is the conscious enjoyer who stays unchanged, like a mountain, while bodies perish.
Embodied souls in the material world are perishable, bound to repeated birth and death, while liberated souls in God's abode have immortal bodies and are imperishable.

verses.devanagari:
उत्तमः पुरुषस्त्वन्यः परमात्मेत्युदाहृतः ।
यो लोकत्रयमाविश्य बिभर्त्यव्यय ईश्वरः॥
verses.transliteration:
uttamaḥ puruṣastvanyaḥ paramātmetyudāhṛtaḥ
yo lokatrayamāviśya bibhartyavyaya īśvaraḥ
verses.essence: But the highest Purusha is yet another, called the supreme Self — the imperishable Lord who, entering the three worlds, sustains them.
verses.translation: But distinct is the Supreme Purusha called the highest Self, the indestructible Lord Who, pervading the three worlds, sustains them.

anvaya.parts: परम (supreme) + आत्मन् (self): the highest Self

anvaya.base: thus; marks a name or quotation
√हृ with उत् + आ · to declare, cite

anvaya.parts: लोक (world) + त्रय (triad): the set of three worlds

verses.explanation: The third term: uttamaḥ puruṣas tv anyaḥ — *another*, beyond both the changing world and the changeless witness. Not the flux, not the stillness watching the flux, but the Lord who enters and carries both: āviśya bibharti, pervading and bearing. The two-story universe of Sankhya gains its missing resident — the owner of the whole house.
verses.connection: The doctrinal peak of the chapter: above matter and above spirit-as-witness stands the sustaining Lord.
verses.reflection: Then remember the third: not the flux, not the witness, but the Lord who enters and carries both.
verses.background: The summit of the chapter and one of the Gita's peaks: two Persons in the world, the perishable (all beings) and the imperishable (the unchanging) — but there is another, the Highest, called Paramatma, the imperishable Lord who enters and sustains the three worlds. Because I transcend the perishable and exceed even the imperishable, I am celebrated as Purushottama. Who knows Me thus, undeluded, worships Me with his whole being — and with this most secret teaching declared, one becomes wise and fulfilled.
verses.hook: Who stands beyond both the perishable and the imperishable?

views.text: The supreme Person is untouched by both adjuncts, the mutable and the immutable; eternal, pure, conscious and free, He upholds the three worlds merely by being present.
The three worlds are non-conscient matter, selves bound to matter, and liberated selves. The Lord enters all three as their Self and supports them, so He is a category distinct from all three.
As Self He differs from inert matter, the perishable; as supreme He differs from the conscious enjoyer, the imperishable; unchanging, He rules and sustains the three worlds.
The Supreme Soul is distinct from the individual soul, which refutes non-dualism; he accompanies each soul through every birth, recording its karmas and granting their results.

verses.devanagari:
यस्मात्क्षरमतीतोऽहमक्षरादपि चोत्तमः ।
अतोऽस्मि लोके वेदे च प्रथितः पुरुषोत्तमः॥
verses.transliteration:
yasmātkṣaramatīto'hamakṣarādapi cottamaḥ
ato'smi loke vedeca prathitaḥ puruṣottamaḥ
verses.essence: Since I transcend the perishable and am higher even than the imperishable, I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as Purushottama — the Supreme Person.
verses.translation: As I transcend the perishable and am even higher than the imperishable, I am declared to be the highest Purusha in the world and in the Vedas.

anvaya.form: relative pronoun, ablative singular, used as a conjunction (because)
adjective used as noun, masculine, accusative singular (object)
adjective used as noun, masculine, ablative singular (than)

anvaya.parts: पुरुष (person) + उत्तम (highest): the highest among persons

verses.explanation: The self-identification the chapter is named for: the speaker is the third purusha. Atītaḥ... uttamaḥ — past the perishing world, and *higher even than the imperishable*. The charioteer holding the reins is declaring himself beyond both everything that changes and everything that doesn't. Etymology becomes theology: puruṣa-uttama, the uttermost Person, a title already celebrated in the world and in the Veda.
verses.connection: Krishna steps into 15.17's vacancy by name — the verse that crowns the Gita's theology of the personal God.
verses.reflection: Address the Purushottama once by full title today — higher than the perishable, above the imperishable.
verses.background: The summit of the chapter and one of the Gita's peaks: two Persons in the world, the perishable (all beings) and the imperishable (the unchanging) — but there is another, the Highest, called Paramatma, the imperishable Lord who enters and sustains the three worlds. Because I transcend the perishable and exceed even the imperishable, I am celebrated as Purushottama. Who knows Me thus, undeluded, worships Me with his whole being — and with this most secret teaching declared, one becomes wise and fulfilled.
verses.hook: Why is Krishna called the Supreme Person in the Vedas?

refs.note: Declares Krishna the Supreme Lord and Supreme Being, to be meditated on, worshipped and served.

views.text: The perishable is the tree of Māyā and the imperishable is its seed; the Lord is beyond both. Devotees know Him so, and poets use the name Puruṣottama.
'Loka' here means Smṛti, since it leads to the Veda's meaning; so the title Supreme Person is found in both Smṛti and Śruti, as in Chāndogya 8.12.3.
One who takes the body for the Self sees the soul as perishing; rightly realized, the I-consciousness is the one pervading all, beyond the insentient elements and without duality.
He is beyond the inert because He is eternally free, and higher than the conscious selves because He is their controller.
By speaking of himself as "I", Krishna shows that he himself is the Supreme Person beyond both perishable and imperishable; other divine forms are manifestations of the same God.

verses.devanagari:
यो मामेवमसम्मूढो जानाति पुरुषोत्तमम् ।
स सर्वविद्भजति मां सर्वभावेन भारत॥
verses.transliteration:
yo māmevamasammūḍho jānāti puruṣottamam
sa sarvavidbhajati māṃ sarvabhāvena bhārata
verses.essence: One who, undeluded, knows me thus as the Supreme Person — that knower of all worships me with whole being, Bharata.
verses.translation: He who, undeluded, knows Me thus as the highest Purusha, he, knowing all, worships Me with his whole being (heart), O Arjuna.

anvaya.parts: अ (not) + सम्मूढ (confused): free from delusion
पुरुष (person) + उत्तम (highest): the highest among persons
सर्व (all) + विद् (knower): one who knows everything
सर्व (all) + भाव (being, feeling): with every part of one's being

verses.explanation: The response right knowledge produces: sarva-vit, such a one knows *everything that matters* — because the root of all has been found — and the knowing immediately overflows as bhajati, worship, sarva-bhāvena, with every fiber, every mood, the whole of one's being. In this chapter's logic, complete theology and complete love are the same event seen from two sides.
verses.connection: The fruit of 15.18: when the Supreme Person is truly known, whole-being devotion is not commanded but inevitable.
verses.reflection: Let right knowing overflow correctly today: worship with the whole being, sarva-bhavena, in one act.
verses.background: The summit of the chapter and one of the Gita's peaks: two Persons in the world, the perishable (all beings) and the imperishable (the unchanging) — but there is another, the Highest, called Paramatma, the imperishable Lord who enters and sustains the three worlds. Because I transcend the perishable and exceed even the imperishable, I am celebrated as Purushottama. Who knows Me thus, undeluded, worships Me with his whole being — and with this most secret teaching declared, one becomes wise and fulfilled.
verses.hook: What does someone who truly knows the Supreme Person do?

refs.note: The one Absolute Truth is known in three ways: as Brahman, Paramātmā and Bhagavān.

views.text: Knowing the Lord as his own Self, he becomes all-knowing through identity with all, and worships with his mind fixed on the Lord as the Self of all.
Sarva-bhāvena means by every prescribed mode of worship; all the love the Lord feels toward every kind of worshipper is roused in Him, in one, toward this knower.
Whatever he perceives he experiences as the Lord's own form, so every action and thought becomes praise and worship without effort.
Reads the order as cause and result: being certain, he worships the Lord in every way, and through that worship becomes all-knowing.
God is realized as formless Brahman, as the Supreme Soul within, and as the personal Bhagavān; knowing and worshipping him as Bhagavān is the most complete knowledge.

verses.devanagari:
इति गुह्यतमं शास्त्रमिदमुक्तं मयानघ ।
एतद्बुद्ध्वा बुद्धिमान्स्यात्कृतकृत्यश्च भारत॥
verses.transliteration:
iti guhyatamaṃ śāstramidamuktaṃ mayānagha
etadbuddhvā buddhimānsyātkṛtakṛtyaśca bhārata
verses.essence: Thus has this most secret teaching been declared by me, sinless one. Awakening to this, one becomes truly wise, Bharata — one whose work is done.
verses.translation: Thus, this most secret science has been taught by Me, O sinless one; on knowing this, a man becomes wise, and all his duties are accomplished, O Arjuna.

anvaya.parts: अ (without) + अघ (sin): one without sin
कृत (done) + कृत्य (what must be done): one who has done all there is to do

verses.explanation: The colophon of a chapter only twenty verses long: guhyatamam śāstram, the *most* secret of teachings — the inverted tree, the fragment-soul, the indwelling fire, the three purushas, all in twenty verses. And the reward is a word every weary person understands: kṛta-kṛtyaḥ — the one whose to-do list is finished forever, who has done the thing all other doings were circling. The search itself retires.
verses.connection: Seals the chapter as a complete scripture-in-miniature — before ch16 turns to those who refuse it.
verses.reflection: Read this chapter's twenty verses sometime as one breath — a complete scripture in miniature.
verses.background: The summit of the chapter and one of the Gita's peaks: two Persons in the world, the perishable (all beings) and the imperishable (the unchanging) — but there is another, the Highest, called Paramatma, the imperishable Lord who enters and sustains the three worlds. Because I transcend the perishable and exceed even the imperishable, I am celebrated as Purushottama. Who knows Me thus, undeluded, worships Me with his whole being — and with this most secret teaching declared, one becomes wise and fulfilled.
verses.hook: What does understanding this teaching do for a person?

views.text: 'Śāstra' names this chapter, in praise: it holds in brief the meaning of the whole Gita and the purport of the Vedas, and knowing it, all duties are fulfilled.
Knowing the teaching of the Supreme Person fulfils all that must be cultivated and done to reach Him, everything except the direct vision of the Lord itself.
Most secret because it teaches the oneness of all. Iti marks the end of the teaching; chapter 16 adds nothing new and only confirms Arjuna's fitness.
Takes 'this most secret śāstra' as the whole scripture, not merely the twenty-verse chapter; whoever understands it becomes fulfilled, and Arjuna all the more.
Krishna sums up the chapter as the essence of the hidden Vedic knowledge, from the nature of the world to the Supreme Person, and promises that those who take it up will reach God-realization.
